title: Given a list of sentences, split each into words and return a flat list of all unique words.
shortTitle: Given a list of sentences, split each into words and return a flat list of all unique words

s1_definition.profdef: This combines `flatMap` with `distinct()`. Each sentence is split into an array of words, turned into a stream, and flatMapped into one flat stream of all words; `distinct()` then removes duplicates to leave each unique word once.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This combines `flatMap` with `distinct()`. Each sentence is split into an array of words, turned into a stream, and flatMapped into one flat stream of all words; `distinct()` then removes duplicates to leave each unique word once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The documentation officer at the National Bank of India has several policy sentences and wants the vocabulary list — every distinct word used, each listed once. She breaks every sentence into words, throws them all into one pile, then removes repeats. `flatMap` makes the single pile and `distinct` removes the repeats.

**One line to remember:** `flatMap` the split words into one stream, then `distinct()` to keep each word once.

sections.s2_technical:
Splitting a sentence gives an array of words, for example `sentence.split("\\s+")`, where the pattern matches one or more whitespace characters so multiple spaces do not produce empty tokens. Each array becomes a stream with `Arrays.stream(...)`, and flatMap concatenates all those per-sentence streams into one flat stream of words.

So the pipeline is sentences.stream, then flatMap of sentence to Arrays.stream of its split words, then distinct, then collect. The flatMap flattens the one level of nesting — sentences holding words — into a single word stream, exactly as with nested collections, except the inner collection here is produced on the fly by splitting.

For a genuinely useful vocabulary you usually normalise the words first, lower-casing them so The and the count as the same word, and often trimming punctuation so word and word-with-a-comma are not treated as different. You would insert a map that lower-cases, and possibly strips non-letters, before the distinct. Without normalisation distinct treats differently-cased or punctuated forms as separate words.

A senior nuance: splitting on whitespace with the regular expression is simple but language-naive. For real text processing — stemming, handling contractions, Unicode word boundaries — you would use a proper tokenizer. For the common interview and reporting case, whitespace split with lower-casing is the pragmatic and correct answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's documentation team wants a vocabulary index of all distinct words used across a set of policy sentences, to check terminology consistency. The sentences are separate strings, and the same word appears many times across them. This is exactly how flatMap plus distinct works — each sentence is split into words, all words are flattened into one stream, normalised to lower case, and distinct keeps each unique word once.

The code works with a list of sentence strings. A `VocabularyService` exposes `uniqueWords(List<String>)` using flatMap over split words, a lower-casing map, and distinct. The runnable `Main` feeds overlapping sentences and logs the unique vocabulary.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three sentences — "Transfer the amount today", "Transfer completed today", "Verify the amount".

Step 1: The stream opens over three sentences.

Step 2: The first sentence enters flatMap. Splitting on whitespace gives Transfer, the, amount, today, which becomes a stream of four words.

Step 3: The second sentence splits into Transfer, completed, today. The third splits into Verify, the, amount. flatMap concatenates all three word streams into one flat stream of ten words.

Step 4: The map lower-cases each word, so Transfer becomes transfer, Verify becomes verify, and so on, so that differently-cased forms will collapse together.

Step 5: distinct walks the flat stream and keeps the first occurrence of each word: transfer, the, amount, today, then completed (new), then verify (new). Repeats like the second transfer, the second today, the second the, and the second amount are dropped.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the unique words in encounter order.

```
Oct 30, 2026 12:25:03 PM com.bank.vocab.service.VocabularyService uniqueWords
INFO: Building vocabulary from 3 sentences
Oct 30, 2026 12:25:03 PM com.bank.vocab.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Unique vocabulary: [transfer, the, amount, today, completed, verify]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: ["Transfer the amount today", "Transfer completed today", "Verify the amount"]
    │
    ▼
  flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split("\\s+")))
    ├─ "Transfer the amount today" → [Transfer, the, amount, today] ─┐
    ├─ "Transfer completed today"  → [Transfer, completed, today] ───┤ concat
    └─ "Verify the amount"         → [Verify, the, amount] ──────────┤
                                                                     ▼
  Flat Stream<String>: Transfer the amount today Transfer completed today Verify the amount
    │
    ▼
  map(toLowerCase)  → transfer the amount today transfer completed today verify the amount
    │
    ▼
  distinct()  → [transfer, the, amount, today, completed, verify]
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [transfer, the, amount, today, completed, verify]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To get the unique words across many sentences I combine flatMap with distinct. I split each sentence into an array of words, turn that array into a stream, and flatMap concatenates all those per-sentence word streams into one flat stream of every word. Then distinct removes the repeats so each word survives exactly once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this built a vocabulary index across a set of policy sentences, so the documentation team could check terminology consistency. The same words appeared across many sentences, so flatMap flattened them all into one stream and distinct collapsed the repeats.

A senior point I always add is normalisation. Before distinct I lower-case every word, otherwise a capitalised The at the start of a sentence and a lowercase the in the middle would be treated as two different words. In richer text I would also strip punctuation so a word followed by a comma is not counted separately. I split on the whitespace regular expression matching one or more spaces, which avoids empty tokens from double spaces, but I am aware that whitespace splitting is language-naive — for real natural-language processing with stemming and Unicode word boundaries I would use a proper tokenizer. For a reporting vocabulary index, split plus lower-case plus distinct is the pragmatic and correct answer.
